title.narrative: Break Free! Mozambique

description.narrative: Empowering adolescents to claim their SRHR rights, supported by civil society, will be achieved if CSOs, youth-led groups and networks are strengthened to lobby and advocate for improved legislation and to promote social norm change in favour of the prevention of CEFMU/TP. Education opportunities and a community supportive of girls’ education will stimulate adolescent girls at risk of TP/CEFMU to access and remain in school, while promoting the re-entrance of girls who have discontinued school due to pregnancy. In order to create a supportive and improved socio-cultural environment that promotes education for girls and SRHR for young people, relevant gate keepers, teachers and parents will be made aware of the importance of adopting attitudes favourable to keeping girls in school. Supporting CSOs to organise, participate and communicate enables CSOs to claim better education and SRHR outcomes for girls and young women, and influence decision-making processes. Duty bearers and decision-makers are made aware of and encouraged to take action to fulfil the education needs of girls based on the effective lobby and advocacy of civil society. Decision-makers at local, national, regional and continental level will be sensitized to build linkages between the levels resulting that civil society is able to elevate issues to higher decision-making levels, and vice versa, they can hold lower-level policy makers and duty bearers accountable for implementing decisions taken at higher levels. This will be enabled by establishing participation and accountability mechanisms between decision-makers/duty bearers and civil society with the support of enhanced youth agency.

SUMMARY Millions of young people don’t have access to appropriate, gender-responsive, quality SRHR education, information and services. This makes them vulnerable to unintended pregnancies, often followed by child marriage (CM). The Break Free! programme empowers adolescents and young people to make their own free and informed choices to speak out and have control over their SRH and lives. BF! is tackling root causes of gender inequality, unequal power relations and discriminatory social norms, systems, structures, policies and practices, supported by civil society and improved legislation. The project will be implemented between 2021 and 2025 by the Break Free! Consortium consisting of Plan International Netherlands, SAT and FAWE, technical partners KIT and RMT in collaboration with Netherlands’ Embassies. It will be carried out in Ethiopia, Kenya, Sudan, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger and a regional Pan-African component to sustain the country programmes.

The prevention of CEFMU and Teenage Pregnancies (TP) is more urgent than ever, as COVID-19 situation has dramatically changed the context in which adolescent girls live resulting in increasing levels of GBV, increasing unpaid care work, rising sexual exploitation, decreased access to education and increasing rates of CEFMU and TP. This crisis has further isolated and excluded adolescent girls in remote areas from accessing SRHR information and services, especially concerning contraception and other essential SRH services. Lockdown restrictions and enforcement of COVID-19 prevention methods have led to an increase in harmful practices such as CEFMU, reducing the effectiveness of referral pathways for essential services, and resulting in poorer SRH outcomes for girls. The loss of employment and income by parents and caregivers is expected to increase girls’ school dropout and girls’ vulnerability to sexual exploitation, resulting in TP and Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs), including HIV. This economic downturn will likely have a large impact on the poverty levels in Nampula province where CEFMU is most prevalent ( 48%). Because poverty is a key driver of CEFMU, these economic impacts are anticipated to increase rates of CEFMU and TP in vulnerable communities. The manipulation of cultural initiation practices has also played a role in encouraging early sex and marriage in Mozambique. Cultural practices, religious beliefs (around contraception) and the inability to have conversations about sexual reproductive health rights (SRHR) makes girls vulnerable to unprotected sex, TP and ultimately CEFMU. Girls and boys are shamed for TP, which leads them to drop out of school.

The programme is a.o. based upon the results and findings of the 18+ ECM ( 2014-2015) and YID programme (2015-2020), implemented by Plan in Mozambique and 6 other countries, combined with experience of FAWE and SAT’s programmes on this theme. All partners have experience on improving legislation and policies on CEFMU and implementation thereof, through L&A and enhancing adolescent’s skills to claim their SRH rights, quality of SRH education, information and service provision. This resulted a.o. into the development of the Southern Africa Development Community (SADC) Model Law on Eradicating Child Marriage, served as legal framework for national law and policy-makers and was used as civil society (CS) advocacy tool across the SADC region. It resulted as well in strengthened CSOs, youth hubs and girls clubs, which have become promoters of ASRHR. Networking between CSOs and CSOs’ access to decision-maker platforms is nevertheless often inadequate in Mozambique to effectively influence, while youth groups face legal challenges as “under the age of 18, adolescents are not allowed to form youth organisations in Mozambique. Since October 2018’s municipal elections, the space for civil society in Mozambique has deteriorated and CSO members suffer physical attacks when discoursing on sensitive issues such as gender policies. By establishing participation and accountability mechanisms between decision makers and civil society with the support of enhanced youth agency, political will increases and civil society has the capacity to advocate for improved SRHR, CM and education related policies, laws and resourcing.

description.narrative: The National Family Law should be revised to prevent marriage before the age of eighteen. Currently, there is no alignment between the Family Law and the law that punishes premature unions (2019) with regard to the concept of child. Family law stipulates that a girl can marry if she is 16 years old and with the consent of her parents. However, law 19/2019 argues that premature unions even with parental consent is a crime. The National Strategy for Preventing and Combating Child Marriages must urgently be reviewed and make marriage before the age of eighteen in all circumstances illegal. And national policies must align, ie: if the National Education System (SNE) recommends that the 12th grade must be completed at least at 17 years, it is inconceivable that family law and early marriages allow a girl to marry at 16, even before completing the cycle.

So far, during the time under review (2.5 year) , there have been no changes in new laws and there has not been any improved commitments.

As from the midterm result no law/policies has been amended or improved, for the next two year the program will focus more on L&A at the provincial and local level and on strengthening CSOs, including youth-led groups, to advocate for effective implementation of the existing laws (Law 19/2019, Law for the prevention and combat of CM and Law 18/ 2018 that advocates free education up to 9th grade).

description.narrative: O2-3: Number of (international) commitments, laws, policies, strategies and bylaws that respond to adolescents' SRHR and education needs being implemented

comment.narrative: The National Family law, which punishes premature unions, and other SRHR and education laws and policies are not known by communities and not enforced by district level governments. There are no district level annual or action plans that speak to the National Strategy for Preventing and Combating Child Marriages. At the district level, key government sectors of Justice, Health, Education and social welfare will be engaged to develop annual plans for the implementation of the National Family Law, the law on Child Marriage and the National Strategy for Preventing and Combating Child Marriages as well as other policies and laws on SRHRs. A technical group, including district focal points from the key government sectors will be established to support monitoring of the implementation of laws and its related sectoral polices and strategies. Budgets (school support fund) made available at the school level do not meet the needs of girls for re-integration after pregnancy, the consortium will advocate for appropriate budget allocation. The consortium is investigating if and how community courts play a role in issues around CM and the programme is exploring if and how they can work with community courts.

7 youth led CSOs (15 - 25 years old) will have their lobby & advocacy capacities strengthened by the programme. In terms of the specific needs related to lobby and advocacy, the CSOs identified the following areas: knowledge on SRHR legislation, SRHR basic concepts and information, and mobilization and engagement skills. Actions such as linking local youth-led groups with district/provincial media to support lobbying and advocacy on girls' education and CM/TP prevention.

It was not possible to achieve this target due to difficulties in understanding the instrument used to report capacity building by CSOs. As discussed during the MTR, the capability assessment tools is very technical making it difficult for organizations to complete and provide detailed information, and some choose not to complete it.
No target set for 2021 as we just started to build capacity of youth led organization
No actual measured as we only comenced capacity building
targeted youth led CSOs to be strengthened

The CSO's reported on include 15 (informal) Adolescent Networks and the 3 second tier in country consortium members. Their capacities and expertise was developed to equip them to be able to in future perform political roles and to implementing advocacy strategies. The adolescent networks received training on knowledges and skills related to lobby and advocacy work and were guided to develop action plans, focusing on L&A natured activities within their communities. In order for the second tier CSO to improve their capacity, they received training on L&A knowledge and skills with a specific link to applying this towards L&A of the key BF thematic teams. Also, training was provided for PME tools that can be used to measure the progress made such as a one day training on Outcome Harvesting. The adolescent networks and CSO's showed to have improved their capacity. This was showcased through the quality of the developed advocacy plans, the carried out interventions by the trained partners and through monitoring of the results of these interventions. The desired future capacity is not considered to be fully achieved. Therefore, ongoing strengthening in the areas of improvement has been planned in for 2023.

In terms of the specific needs related to lobby and advocacy, the CSOs identified the following areas: knowledge on SRHR legislation, SRHR basic concepts and information, and mobilization and engagement skills.

The challenging political landscape since the 2023 elections, marked by ongoing insecurity and a restricted civic space, has significantly hindered the L&A efforts of various CSOs, including youth-led groups. As a result, progress in strengthening their L&A capacities has been slow, despite valuable lessons learned along the way.

The Consortium will conduct lobby and advocacy efforts by increasing the capacity and enhancing budget tracking and lobbying for increased funding for SRHR services at all level, and review of the teacher code conduct based on the partners' organizational capacity assessments. All partners will rely on various research-based information to support Lobby and Advocacy initiatives.
